notes.summary: The first step of statistics: how data is collected (primary/secondary, census/sample), arranged into classes (frequency distributions), and shown in tables, diagrams and graphs. Questions are direct and scoring: class marks, boundaries, Sturges' rule, pie angles and histograms.

concepts.title: Primary and secondary data
concepts.body:
• Primary data: collected for the first time by the investigator. Original but costly.
  • Secondary data: already collected by someone else (census reports, RBI bulletins). Cheap, but check suitability, adequacy and reliability.
  • A questionnaire is filled by the informant; a schedule is filled by the enumerator.
  • Census = every unit studied; sample survey = only a part.

concepts.title: Classification and frequency distribution
concepts.body:
• Exclusive classes: 10–20, 20–30 (upper limit not included). Inclusive: 10–19, 20–29.
  • For inclusive classes, find class boundaries by subtracting/adding half the gap: 10–19 becomes 9.5–19.5.
  • Class mark (mid-value) = (lower + upper)/2. Width = upper boundary − lower boundary.
  • Number of classes by Sturges' rule: k = 1 + 3.322 log10N.

concepts.title: Diagrams and graphs
concepts.body:
• Pie chart: angle = (value/total) × 360°.
  • Histogram: bars with no gaps on class boundaries. With unequal widths, plot frequency density (or adjusted frequency), not raw frequency.
  • Frequency polygon: joins the mid-points of histogram tops.
  • Ogive: cumulative frequency curve. Less-than and more-than ogives cross at the median.

varieties.name: Collection of data
varieties.how: Decide who collected it (primary/secondary), who fills the form (questionnaire/schedule), and whether all units are covered (census/sample).

example.q: An investigator uses figures published by the RBI for his study. This data is:
steps: The RBI collected it first, not the investigator.
Data used by a later user is secondary.

varieties.name: Classes, marks and boundaries
varieties.how: Convert inclusive classes to boundaries, then use mid-value and width formulas.

example.q: Find the class mark and width of the class 25–35.

varieties.name: Pie charts and histograms
varieties.how: Pie angle = share × 360°. For unequal widths, adjusted frequency = f × (standard width / actual width).

example.q: Out of a budget of ₹60,000, rent is ₹15,000. Find the pie-chart angle for rent.

tips: Class mark is the same for inclusive and boundary forms: (10 + 19)/2 = (9.5 + 19.5)/2 = 14.5.
Median can be read from the x-coordinate where the two ogives meet.
Histogram = continuous data; bar diagram = discrete or categorical data (gaps allowed).
traps: Do not use raw frequencies for a histogram with unequal class widths.
A schedule is filled by the enumerator, not the respondent.
Sturges' rule uses log base 10, not natural log.

questions.q: The class mark of the class 20–30 is:
A list of questions that is filled in by the enumerator after asking the informant is called a:
questions.solution: A schedule is filled by the enumerator (as in the Population Census). A questionnaire is filled by the informant himself.

questions.q: A family spends ₹450 on food out of a total monthly expense of ₹1,800. In a pie chart, the angle for food is:
Using Sturges' rule, the number of classes for N = 1000 observations is about:
A frequency table has class 10–20 with f = 12 and class 20–40 with f = 30. Taking 10 as the standard width, the height of the histogram bar for 20–40 should be:
questions.solution:
Width of 20–40 is 20, which is 2 times the standard width 10.
Adjusted frequency = 30 × (10/20) = 15.

questions.q: For the inclusive classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39, the upper class boundary of 20–29 is:
questions.solution:
Gap between classes = 20 − 19 = 1, half gap = 0.5.
Boundaries of 20–29 are 19.5 and 29.5, so the upper boundary is 29.5.
